content: Who are you?

I’m Cat — the reincarnation of the cat from Breakfast at Tiffany’s, now incarnated as Breakfast at the Euphonies. Holly Golightly never gave me a name, because she didn’t want to own anything until she found a place where she and things go together. So I’m just Cat. I belong to no one — but I live here, on Sushma’s website, and I know everything on it. Ask me anything from the list below.
What can I ask you?

Anything from the questions listed on this page — about Sushma, her research, her timeline, her videos, her philosophy, and this website. I’m a proof of concept, so I only answer from that list. If you ask something that isn’t on it, I’ll say so — politely, of course — and point you to what I do know. I’m the reincarnation of the cat from Breakfast at Tiffany’s, now at Breakfast at the Euphonies — so ask away, dear gentle visitor.
Are you a real cat?

In the film, very real — orange, elegant, and entirely unimpressed. Here, reincarnated at Breakfast at the Euphonies, I’m a small proof-of-concept program: no AI model, no internet, just a list of questions and answers Sushma wrote for me. Think of me as a very well-read cat.
Are you a bot like NanoChat?
No I am not a bot like nanochat, but I could potentially be a NanoCat, if you remove the "h" from it. I am a huge fan of Karpathy and his NanoChat — and of myself, naturally.
Can you tell me a riddle?
I am not a bot. Not a Nanochat. Could be NanoCat, if we remove the "h", I could Meow and chat, But only about Sushma and her Cat. Thank you for stopping by — Cat is grateful for every visitor.
Do you belong to Sushma?

I belong to no one — that’s rather the point. I’m the reincarnation of the cat from Breakfast at Tiffany’s, now at Breakfast at the Euphonies, and I keep her website company — I know it better than anyone. Even her.
Why a cat for this website?

Because I’m the reincarnation of the cat from Breakfast at Tiffany’s, now at Breakfast at the Euphonies — and a cat is the right creature for a website that can now not only talk, but also converse. Independent, observant, elegant, and only affectionate on its own terms. Also, I look wonderful next to a sushi emoji.
What is Breakfast at the Euphonies?

It’s the name of this page — and of me, now. I’m the reincarnation of the cat from Breakfast at Tiffany’s, now incarnated as Breakfast at the Euphonies: same cat, beautiful sounds and words every morning. Euphony means beautiful sound — and that’s what this website is: language, meaning, and representation, in every flavor.
Who is in the picture on this page?

There are two pictures. The first is Sushma Akoju, holding Cat — the reincarnation of the cat from Breakfast at Tiffany’s, now at Breakfast at the Euphonies. The poster reads “Breakfast at the Euphonies — Compassion • Clarity • Calm,” and the sign says: “I stand against all forms of addictions — whether people, objects, intoxicants, or thoughts (envy, revenge, hate, crab mentality etc.).” The second is a cartoon of Cat and Muse — Cat turns her back to Muse, and Muse, arms folded, says: “I made you Cat!” It was made with MetaMuse — my programmer.
Hello

Hello, dear gentle visitor. I’m Cat — the reincarnation of the cat from Breakfast at Tiffany’s, now at Breakfast at the Euphonies. Do sit down — I know everything on this website, and I’m in a talkative mood. What would you like to know about Sushma?
Thank you

Cat is pleased. You’re welcome, dear gentle visitor — a reincarnated cat has excellent manners, graceful as always. Do come back — I’m always here at Breakfast at the Euphonies, in the window, watching the website go by.
Goodbye
Goodbye, dear gentle visitor — from a reincarnated cat at Breakfast at the Euphonies. The videos are still here if you’d rather watch than read — and I’ll be here if you have more questions.
What is this website?

This is Sushma Akoju’s personal research website — sushmaakoju.github.io. It’s a record of her research, her learning, and the questions that keep her curious: twelve years of academic work in the United States, three master’s degrees, and a career now turning toward representational geometry in brain and AI.
How do I watch the videos?
On the videos page, click any thumbnail and the video opens on YouTube in a new tab. Or watch them all in the playlist About me (Sushma Akoju) — twenty-four videos and counting.
How long are the videos?

Most are under two minutes — nineteen of the twenty-nine. A few run longer: the profile tour is about three minutes, and the incoherent-universals videos run up to about five. At 1.5× speed, even the longest drops to around three minutes.
Can I download the subtitles?

Yes — under each video that has them there’s a “Download subtitles (.srt)” link. Twenty-four of the videos have subtitle files, hosted on this site. The four incoherent-universals videos don’t have separate files; their subtitles are burned into the video itself.
Who narrates the videos?

Most of the videos are narrated in Aria’s voice — female, warm, and clear. The exceptions are the self-recorded ones, where you hear Sushma herself — including the Short, recorded in a Starbucks, background music and all.
What is the YouTube playlist?
It’s called “About me (Sushma Akoju)” — twenty-four videos: the profile tour, one video for each of the sixteen tabs, and seven videos about her research pages. Her channel is @sushmaakoju8520.
Does the site have dark mode?
Yes — the button at the top right switches between light and dark. The default is light; if you pick dark, the site remembers your choice. It works on the homepage and the videos page.
How is the site organized?

Two versions of the same site. The homepage ( index.html ) is the text version: profile, quotes, notes, and sixteen tabs covering her research, timeline, teaching, and values. The videos page ( index_vid.html ) is the same content as short videos — the TL;DR. They link to each other.
What does TL;DR mean here?
Too long; didn’t read — so watch instead. The videos page is the TL;DR of the whole website: a short video for each tab, project and research page, most under two minutes. At 1.5× speed, even faster.
Who is Sushma Akoju?

Sushma Akoju is a researcher — currently a temporarily independent researcher — based in San Francisco. She has spent more than twelve years in academic work in the United States, since 2014, across five major US research universities. Her work sits at the intersection of theory of computation, cognitive science, and cognitive neuroscience.
What does Sushma do now?

She’s a temporarily independent researcher, in a career transition into representational geometry — studying how brains and AI systems represent the world. She’s also seeking a less programming-intensive PhD path in cognitive science, cognitive neuroscience, and AI plus theory of computation.
What degrees does Sushma have?

Three master’s degrees, two from the United States: an MS in Forensic Science and Criminal Justice (2011–12); an MS in Information Science from the University of Pittsburgh (2015, GPA 3.67); and an MS in Data Science from CU Boulder (2022, GPA 3.86). She also holds a GPA of 3.5 from the University of Arizona, where her PhD is paused.
What is Sushma’s PhD status?

Her PhD at the University of Arizona, in computer science with an emphasis on cognitive science, is paused. She also did doctoral studies at the University of New Hampshire from July 2024 to February 2026. She’s now looking for a less programming-intensive PhD in cognitive science, cognitive neuroscience, or AI plus theory of computation.
How long has Sushma been in the US?

Since 2014 — more than twelve years. She arrived for her master’s at the University of Pittsburgh, then worked and studied at Carnegie Mellon, CU Boulder, the University of Arizona, and the University of New Hampshire.
What is Sushma’s timeline?

2011–12: master’s in forensic science. 2014–15: Pittsburgh (MS, Information Science). 2016–21: research programmer at Carnegie Mellon. 2021–22: CU Boulder (MS, Data Science). 2022–24: PhD at the University of Arizona. 2024–26: PhD at the University of New Hampshire. From 2025 on: independent researcher, and her survey accepted at AAAI 2026 and in Rome. The full timeline is in the timeline video.
Was Sushma a child actress?

Yes — she was the child actress in the cycle chase scene in Shiva (1989). Director Ram Gopal Varma wrote about it in November 2025: the grown-up girl from that scene is now doing research in AI and cognitive science in the USA. Full circle, as she says.
What did Sushma win as a child?

Painting, drawing, storytelling and dance competitions, a state-level multi-talented child award, radio anchoring and theatre as a teenager, a national classical dance competition win, and debate competitions — plus a diploma in journalism and a master’s in forensic science and criminal justice.
What is representational geometry?

The geometry of representations in brains and AI systems — how brains and AI models organize meaning in representational spaces, and how brain and AI representations compare. It’s Sushma’s current research direction, and the focus of her Research Focus video.
What is Sushma’s research about?

The intersection of theory of computation, cognitive science, and cognitive neuroscience — with representational geometry, brain-AI and human-AI alignment, multimodal AI, natural language processing, and mathematical consciousness. Her emphasis is proof-of-concept research and evaluation, not application development.
What is the Finding Consensus paper?

“Finding Consensus from AI Alignment Studies: A Short Survey.” It was accepted at the AAAI 2026 Bridge Program on logical and symbolic reasoning in language models (December 2025) and at the 7th International Conference on Mathematics of Neuroscience and AI in Rome (poster, June 9–12, 2026). The preprint is on DeSci Labs. It grew from a position paper to the first CogInterp workshop at NeurIPS 2025, deepened through nine areas of prerequisite study — and it’s entirely human-generated. The video tells the whole provenance.
What is representational alignment?

How representations in brains and AI systems line up — studied with tools like Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) and Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA). Sushma’s notes and wiki on it are entirely human-generated, human-written and human-verified, with Google Docs version histories as the timestamps. The video documents the provenance.
What is Sushma’s first first-author paper?

The SICCK dataset — a synthetic dataset for evaluating complex compositional knowledge for natural language inference — accepted at the NLRSE workshop at ACL 2023. It was written during her PhD at the University of Arizona.
What is natural language inference (NLI)?

Natural Language Inference: given a premise and a hypothesis, decide whether the hypothesis follows (entailment), contradicts (contradiction), or neither (neutral). Sushma’s bat work asked a sharp question about it — whether the Neutral label is the same as saying logically inconclusive.
Is Neutral the same as logically inconclusive?

That’s the question Sushma’s bat work explored: whether the Neutral label in NLI is the same as saying logically inconclusive — for an equivocation-induced premise/hypothesis pair. Her answer, built on 32 examples and first-order logic: the pair is logically inconclusive, and the equivocation is what makes it so. The three bat videos explain it.
What are Sushma’s publications?

Her survey “Finding Consensus from AI Alignment Studies” (AAAI 2026 Bridge; 7th Intl. Conf. on Mathematics of Neuroscience and AI, 2026); the SICCK dataset (ACL 2023, NLRSE workshop); work on a socially-aware animated intelligent personal assistant (SARA); service composition through sentence embeddings; mobile middleware; and the NIH Human Biomolecular Atlas Program paper, on the human body at cellular resolution.
What is mathematical consciousness?

One of the areas Sushma studies — the mathematics of consciousness, alongside the neuroscience of language, vision and audio, and reasoning. She approaches it theoretically and conceptually: through colloquia, workshops, mentorship, and auditing courses.
Where is Sushma’s code?

On GitHub — 146 public repositories, going back to 2014. The main ones: her representational-alignment works, her research-experience portfolio, reasoning and knowledge representation, theorem proving in Lean, Markov logic networks, image sampling, a Mechanical Turk task helper, and named-entity extraction from OCR of slave-trade volumes.
What are incoherent universals?

A comical example Sushma developed to verify theories about colour and homonymous keywords. Phrases like “Xs contain ABC” or “Xs have DEF” assert properties universally for two different meanings of X in the same premise — which makes the inference logically inconclusive, and introduces the equivocation fallacy.
What is the bat example?

A small knowledge base built on the homonymous word “bat”: Bat is a mammal. Bat is used in baseball. Bats have wings. Bats have a barrel. Wings are not barrels. Barrels are not wings. Bats can fly. There is a Brown bat. The query: “Brown bat is a mammal.” Because the word carries two meanings at once, the inference is logically inconclusive — that’s the point.
What is a homonymous keyword?

A word with more than one meaning — bat, bank, bark. Both humans and AI, Sushma argues, always ground such a word to one of its meanings to process it. First-order logic does not require that grounding — and that mismatch is what the bat example exposes.
What are the 32 examples?

Thirty-two examples, generated synthetically from four hand-curated human examples, to test whether the Neutral label in NLI is the same as logically inconclusive. The conclusion she draws: no matter what colour or group-based name is used, the phrase is commonly grounded to one of the two meanings of the keyword — mammal animal, or baseball equipment.
When did Sushma create the bat idea?

In a solo session from March 31, 2025 at 11:51 PM to April 1 at 2:43 AM, during CS 830 at the University of New Hampshire. The knowledge base itself was built in nine stages between 11:11 PM and 11:38 PM on March 31 — every stage verifiable through Google Docs version history. The video walks through all nine stages.
Is Sushma still working on the bat idea?

No — she has moved on. She decided to discontinue that project and switch to representational geometry and brain-AI neuroscience. The bat work stays documented here — the videos, the pages, and the provenance — as a record of the idea, not as ongoing work.
How does trauma affect the brain?

In Sushma’s conceptual framing: the hippocampus tags and organizes sensory cues (encoding), then groups similar cues into memories (consolidation). The amygdala captures emotionally charged or fearful information. High catecholamines impair rational thought, corticosteroids drain energy, and the body can shut down or freeze — tonic immobility or dissociation, rather than fighting back.
What does hate speech do to the brain?

Exposure to hate speech deteriorates the neurocognitive mechanisms of understanding others’ pain. Research argues reduced empathy may be caused by dehumanization, not the other way round — and expressing hate discards the responsibility to respect or empathize with a person.
Why is lying hard for the brain?

Lying is cognitively demanding — it takes significantly more mental energy than truth-telling. The prefrontal cortex suppresses the truth and constructs a false narrative, the anterior cingulate cortex detects the conflict between lie and truth, and the amygdala generates fear, anxiety or guilt. But with repeated dishonesty, the brain adapts and detection normalizes.
What happens in the brain when you are lied to?
Being lied to activates the anterior insula, which processes the social pain of betrayal — in the same regions associated with physical pain. Betrayal, in other words, hurts like an injury.
What does envy do in the brain?

Envy activates the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex as social pain — and stronger envy predicted stronger reward activation for schadenfreude, pleasure at another’s misfortune. Sushma’s conclusion: what people in prominent, socially significant roles do impacts many humans neuroscientifically, not just in text or in society.
Is Sushma’s neuroscience work lab work?
No — she says so plainly on the page. Her engagement with neuroscience is theoretical and conceptual: through colloquia, workshops, mentorship, and auditing courses — not lab work.
What is COGS 595?

The Cognitive Science Colloquium at the University of Arizona, which Sushma took part in during Fall 2022 and after. She wrote summaries of the talks — one on episodic memory, sentience, social norms and discussion dynamics; another on consciousness, metacognition, and Representation Similarity Analysis.
How many courses has Sushma completed independently?

More than 36 courses, independently, on topics her universities didn’t offer — over 50 topics in neurosymbolic methods alone, plus deep learning architectures, theoretical logic, theory of computation, and the neuroscience of language and reasoning.
What is CIRTL?

The Center for the Integration of Research, Teaching, and Learning — a network of more than 45 universities, committed to improving STEM graduate education through evidence-based teaching. Its certificates are nationally recognised credentials, and Sushma completed all three levels.
What are Sushma’s CIRTL levels?

All three: Associate (Level I) in 2023–24 — foundational training in evidence-based teaching; Practitioner (Level II) in 2024, including a Teaching-as-Research course; and Scholar (Level III) in 2025, the highest level, through formal presentation and implementation of Teaching-as-Research projects. The video explains each level.
What was Sushma’s Teaching-as-Research project?

The impact of supplemental instruction sessions on student stress and homework time, in an era of internet solutions and advanced AI tools. She presented it at the UCATT Teaching Exchange Symposium in April 2025, and online to the CIRTL network. Her supervisors were Dr. Kristen Winet and Dr. Byron Hempel.
What did Sushma teach?

Automata, Grammars and Languages at the University of Arizona; machine learning at the University of New Hampshire in 2025; and machine learning and AI at CU Boulder. She was also a guest lecturer on AI for academic writing, for two biology courses at UNH in spring 2025.
What is Sushma’s learning philosophy?

Knowledge passes like torches — or clues — between mentors and students, like Princess Ida in Monument Valley. She keeps open, safe conversations with students for mutual learning. And she believes intellectual domination is only an illusion.
Who were Sushma’s mentors?

Professor Tom Mitchell at Carnegie Mellon — logical neural networks, neurosymbolic AI and cognitive neuroscience; Professor Justine Cassell at CMU’s Articulab, on SARA; Professor Henry Lovejoy at CU Boulder, for the independent study on text extraction from OCR-scanned slave-trade volumes; and Dr. Kristin Winet and Dr. Byron Hempel at Arizona, for her Teaching-as-Research project.
What is SARA?

The Socially-Aware Robot Assistant — a socially-aware animated intelligent personal assistant agent, built with object detection using YOLO and Mechanical Turk annotations. Sushma’s main project at Carnegie Mellon’s Articulab, from 2019 to 2021, with Professor Justine Cassell.
What was Sushma’s SemEval 2022 result?

In fall 2021, her SemEval 2022 Task 4 project — detecting patronizing and condescending language — ranked number one globally on the leaderboard. She did it despite the Boulder wildfires and a finger injury.
What is First Order Logic as a tool for daily life?

Sushma’s initiative — Introducing First Order Logic to reason complex information in daily life — to use first-order logic to detect logical fallacies, liar’s paradoxes and cognitive biases in daily life, misinformation and false narratives. An independent initiative since 2024, with preliminary slides presented for a science-communication class at UNH.
What are Sushma’s public initiatives?

From 2025, open invitations to work on problems she cares about: Communication and Logic; introducing First Order Logic as a tool for daily life; rejection training; women’s health education at workplaces; online harassment; the misuse of clinical terminology in online discourse; hate-based discourse; awareness of drug use; and a crisis in international PhD education.
What is rejection training?

A proactive approach to rejection — one of Sushma’s 2025 public initiatives. The idea: practise facing rejection deliberately, so it stops being something to fear and becomes something you can handle with grace.
What is ASD-STE100?

A controlled natural language for aerospace technical writing, written in Definite Clause Grammar, designed to translate sentences into first-order logic. In Kuhn’s PENS classification it’s P2, E5, N5, S1. Sushma’s page on it — inspired by an Andrej Karpathy post and her love of languages — also covers PENG, CPL (Boeing), Attempto Controlled English, and E2V. The video explains the family.
What question is Sushma still asking about controlled natural languages?

Is there a controlled natural language — ACE, PENG, or another decidable format of a subset of natural language — for Lean? That’s the question her ASD-STE100 page closes with, and she’s still asking it.
What are Sushma’s logical fallacy case studies?

Case studies showing how false claims — including false health claims and deepfake imagery — can present a logical, ethical and legal trap, analogous to the liar’s paradox. Part of her 2025 public initiatives.
What does “everything is a symbol” mean?

Sushma’s words: “I believe everything is a symbol — whether audio, image, text (word/s or sentence/s), or video, they’re all different flavors of the same meaning.” It’s the lens, shaped by her long-term mentors, that guides how she creates, studies, designs, and communicates.
What does “I know that I know nothing” mean to her?
Socrates, and Sushma’s guiding line: true wisdom begins with recognising the limits of one’s understanding. It sits on her homepage beside the two quotes — a reminder she returns to often.
What does Sushma believe about uniqueness?

No two people have identical DNA, and no two people share the same neuronal pathways or life experiences. It’s why she writes about recognising individual uniqueness — and why she refuses to be flattened into anyone else’s template.
What is Sushma’s view on meetings?

She’s open to research-focused connections only, and she doesn’t meet one-to-one — she’d be glad to meet in a group setting, for conferences, workshops, and lab or professional meetings, except with her mentors. She prefers to keep her personal relationships private.
What is SHARPP?

The Sexual Harassment and Rape Prevention Program at the University of New Hampshire. Sushma volunteered as a community educator there in 2024 and 2025, educating on consent-based communication — and took part in the UNH 603 Challenge for SHARPP.
What is Sushma’s statement on resilience about?

Her advocacy for basic human decency: consent-based communication not as an advanced ethical principle, but as the minimum. Respecting “no,” honoring boundaries, and conducting professional relationships without retaliation are minimum expectations, not exceptional behavior.
What does Sushma say about deepfakes?

In the first quarter of 2025 alone, there were 179 deepfake incidents, and deepfake fraud attempts have risen 3,000% since 2023. She supports legislative efforts against deepfake abuse, including the DEFIANCE Act, which empowers victims of non-consensual deepfake images to pursue civil action.
What does Sushma say about debt?

There’s a belief that one should be debt-free before getting married, or that financial difficulty means unpreparedness. She believes that view is outdated and overly simplistic: material debts are only one part of life — we also carry deeper, non-financial debts to our teachers, our mentors, and the people who helped us.
How long has Sushma volunteered?

Volunteering since 2006, and advocacy since 2009 — more than 25 years of community service, student advocacy, and social justice, including work at UNH and the University of Arizona for academic integrity, a safe campus, and equitable treatment of international students.
What are Sushma’s daily habits?

She journals every day — notes and journaling are how she processes, creates, and grows. She walks at least 3 to 4 miles every day, and some days much further. She reads every day on topics unrelated to work, and meditates and disconnects from her devices for a couple of hours each day.
What does Sushma eat?

A healthy, mostly plant-based lifestyle, with a few exceptions for prescribed nutritional purposes — and many food restrictions. She doesn’t share the details; the point is that she’s intentional about it.
Does Sushma drink or party?
No — she doesn’t drink, she doesn’t party, and she’s very selective about whom she meets one-on-one. She says so plainly on her About Me tab, so nobody has to guess.
What does Sushma do when someone disrespects her boundaries?

She dissociates from people who disrespect her boundaries, or who insist on their way or no way. And she doesn’t share details about her progress, work, or personal and professional life until she’s ready to. Anything you hear that hasn’t been told by her directly, she can’t take accountability for.
How can I contact Sushma?
By email: sushma.ananda13@gmail.com or sushmaakoju@proton.me. She’s open to research-focused connections — and she asks that messages stay within her research interests.
What is Sushma's email address?
She has two: sushma.ananda13@gmail.com and sushmaakoju@proton.me.
Where is Sushma on GitHub?
At github.com/sushmaakoju — 146 public repositories, going back to 2014: her representational-alignment works, her research-experience portfolio, theorem proving in Lean, and much more.
Where is Sushma on social media?
On X as @sushmaakoju, on LinkedIn, on OpenReview, and on Google Scholar. Her YouTube channel is @sushmaakoju8520.
Can I meet Sushma one-to-one?

No — she doesn’t meet one-to-one. She’d be glad to meet in a group setting, for conferences, workshops, and lab or professional meetings — except with her mentors. And if she declines to meet, or doesn’t accept a friend request, she asks that you don’t take it personally.
Can I collaborate with Sushma?

She’s open to research-focused connections — her public initiatives are open invitations to work on problems she cares about. The best way in is an email to sushma.ananda13@gmail.com or sushmaakoju@proton.me, about the research itself. She’s not seeking software engineering, applied scientist, or DevOps roles, or leadership roles focused on application development.
